newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Aramco to gain from Far East naphtha demand.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Aramco to gain from Far East naphtha demand.

text.p: Saudi Aramco is likely to secure a higher price premium from Far East term lifters of Saudi naphtha for the second half of the year, Gulf traders said on Wednesday.

Most sources at Asian firms based in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring Gulf states were consigned to accept a double-digit premium for Aramco's A-180 paraffinic naphtha grade compared to a $6.50 premium in the first half of 1997.
"It is advisable to accept the higher premium...Customers are not happy but they want the contracts," one source said.
Aramco's clients are expected to submit their bids for second-half supplies by April 4 with bids valid till May 21.
Gulf-based traders would not say what their actual premium or volume bids would be though one company said it was considering bidding below $10 in the initial round.

Rising Asian petrochemical feedstock demand for naphtha and Kuwait Petroleum Corp's (KPC) ability to win a $13.50 premium from its naphtha customers put Aramco in a strong position to ratchet up the premium, traders said.
Aramco and KPC are the largest exporters of Middle East naphtha and their pricing policies, though based on different market formulas, often echo each other.
"How can you risk disagreeing with Aramco on the premium when there is so much demand," said one industry executive.
"Renewing the (naphtha) contract is important...this is not the time to upset supplies," he added.
Aramco sells some 7.2 million tonnes (165,000 barrels per day) of naphtha on term basis from its Ras Tanura, Rabigh and Yanbu and Jubail refineries with 4.5 tonnes going to Asia.
Naphtha is processed through aromatics or ethylene plants in the manufacture of plastics, polyesters and synthetic rubber.

Major Japnese lifters of Saudi A-180 naphtha from Ras Tanura include Marubeni Corp (700,000 tonnes from July 1996-June 1997), Mitsui (600,000 tonnes) and Mitsubishi Chemical (300,000 tonnes), according to the Cyprus-based Middle East Economic Survey (MEES) newsletter.
South Korea's Samsung (200,000 tonnes) and Lucky Goldstar (100,000 tonnes) and Malaysia's Titan (350,000 tonnes) are also major Asian customers of A-180, according to MEES.

Lifters of naphtha in the first half of 1996 paid a $2.40 premium to daily independent price quotations but have seen this premium steadily increase as Aramco and other Gulf exporters in Bahrain and Abu Dhabi capitalised on surging Asian demand.

Naphtha, Aramco's main oil product export alongside fuel oil, was assessed at $203 a tonne fob Gulf on Wednesday with spot premiums running at $14-15, compared to $155 a tonne and $6 a tonne premium in March 1996.
Strong Asian petrochemical demand has been the main factor behind the rally in Gulf naphtha prices and premiums despite new refining capacity coming onstream in Asia.
Higher export prices and persistent strong Asian naphtha demand in Asia prompted Aramco last month to import gasoline so that it could maximise naphtha yields at its refineries.
